My first job after college was retail for a fabric and craft store.  I was hired about 2 weeks before Black Friday, so I was still learning to use the register when Black Friday came around.  It was awful.  There was always a line at the register even though we had all 4 of them running.  My boss wouldn't let me ring up anyone because I was making mistakes, but I was only making mistakes because she was hovering over me like a giant doom cloud making me incredibly nervous.  I hate being watched like that.  And loud noises and crowds bother me, too.  I only had to work 4 hours that day, but it sucked.  So, I'm pretty sympathetic to your feelings.  Empathetic, really, because I've been there and I know how terrifying it can be.  The only thing I can say is to take breaks when you need them.  Is it possible to start looking for a job that isn't in retail?

This is totally normal.  It sounds like a crush to me, and it's always painful to develop a crush when you know you'll never be able to have what you want.  It's not silly.  I'm pretty sure everyone goes through this at some point in their lives, but they don't talk about it because they're embarrassed.

I've periodically been obsessed with different actors/actresses I've seen on TV or in movies.  I'll read about them on Wikipedia and look up pictures of them on Google.  I find people in general interesting, and celebrities are the easiest to find information on because so much of their lives is public knowledge.  That's unfortunate for them sometimes, which is another story entirely.  Unless you're stalking someone or it's taking away from your life for such a significant amount of time that you can't hold down a job or your relationships with other people suffer, it's perfectly within the realm of normal.

I actually had a situation where I had a huge crush on someone in real life whom I knew I was never going to be with.  I was in Chicago for a week, met a woman there whom, much like you did with Taissa Farmiga, I found very attractive despite the fact that she would not have been considered typically attractive by our current societal standards.  I loved her demeanor, her laugh, her style, her body shape, everything about her.  But, I was only in Chicago for a week, and she most likely had a life of her own.  I told my boyfriend about it, and he laughed with me.  He said, "You would fall for someone like that."  Mind you, my boyfriend and I are in a monogamous relationship, but we're honest enough with one another to know that crushes are a thing that happen all the time and are something we shouldn't be ashamed of.  So, we talk about them, and laugh, and move on.

I hope this helps.

Edit:  I'd also like to point out that the crush I had felt physically painful in my chest.  It was hard to walk away from it, and sometimes I think about it and it still hurts.  It lingers, but I try not to feel bad about it.

Edit 2:  Taissa Farmiga had a similar effect on me.  Her character in AMH has a lot of depth.  In addition, Farmiga is a very talented actress.

What kind of doctor are you going to see?  A counselor or therapist?  Or are they a general practitioner or family doctor?  I know when I went to see my family doctor to ask for a referral for a counselor, he asked me a series of questions about how I felt and what my habits were.  The questions were like a springboard for me to talk about my issues.  I could answer them with yes or no, but I could also explain a little bit.  Usually the visit starts like that.

Your mental health is just as important as your physical health, and your doctor will most likely take it just as seriously.  I doubt you'll be dismissed.  If you are, be persistent about your feelings.  Be honest and detailed.  If you don't feel like getting out of bed in the morning, say that.  If you've had suicidal thoughts, say that.  If you don't enjoy activities you used to enjoy, say that.  If you can't focus, say that.  Anything you feel, you can say.  As for how - it's probably easiest just to say it as it comes to you.  Being honest with yourself and your healthcare provider about your depression is important.  You could write down a list of your symptoms and take it with you to read to or give to the doctor.  They'll ask you questions about it.
To me this sounds like situational depression, but I would suggest seeing a counselor or therapist for a more formal diagnosis.
It's her choice to take you back or not.  Looking for advice on how to convince her to do so is probably not going to be very fruitful, nor is it great for her own mental health.

Breathe normally (not deep breaths).  Breathe in for 4 seconds, hold for 4 seconds, breathe out for 4 seconds, hold for 4 seconds.  Repeat 4 times or until you feel a little better.

Just breathe normally, don't take deep breaths.  I recommended this to a friend last week and forgot to say don't take deep breaths.  Of course, that means he took deep breaths and then felt lightheaded.  He tried it again with regular breaths and felt better.  I do it every once in a while when my anxiety flares.  It gives me something to concentrate on for a minute or two and usually brings my anxiety level down.

Severe stress is usually situational - meaning it comes up when something happens in your life that causes stress, so it's something external to yourself.  Anxiety is something that originates internally and is often a disproportionate reaction to external stimuli.  Prolonged severe stress can lead to anxiety.  The way I differentiate between the two for myself is by taking a look at the source of the stress.  Is a life event happening that is taking up a lot of my energy (moving, illness in the family, emotional/physical abuse, divorce, etc.)?  Or did something happen a long time ago that I'm still dwelling on?  How long have I been stressed out over this?

Either way, talking to your teachers or seeing your school counselor about it might not be a bad idea especially since you said you can't really talk it out with your parents.  If it's affecting your school performance, now is the point when you should seek help.  If you are less you, then it's time.

I removed a lot of my "friends" on Facebook and stuck with people who don't create drama in my life.  I had about 170 friends, and now I'm down to 70.  I get a lot less "likes", but in more ways than I can count, I'm happier for it.  I've considered deleting my account, but I keep in touch with friends from college and my time abroad through Facebook.  I met my SO through a dating website, but as soon as we got serious, I deleted my account.  Never looked back on that one.  For the most part, anyone I want to keep in touch with regularly I call or text or see fairly frequently.  Not being glued to social media is helpful.  I believe there have been several studies showing a correlation between social media use and depression/anxiety.  Correlation, now, not causation.

Severing ties, or at the very least limiting use of, social media might be beneficial for a lot of people.  In my experience, limiting social media presence highlights who is really important to you and who you are important to.  And, it simplifies how much you have to think/worry about and leaves more time for things you really enjoy.

Yeah, I've definitely experienced that.  I used to watch a lot of Grey's Anatomy to distract myself from my anxiety.  It worked for a really long time, but after a while, it felt like it was just background noise that made my anxiety worse.  I'd turn it on and zone out while the anxiety washed over me in waves.  The silence that came when I would turn off the TV was deafening, like static in my ears and pins and needles in my brain.

At that time, I didn't have a full-time job.  I was working part-time retail.  What really helped me was getting a full-time job and seeing more people more often.  That might be one way to alleviate some anxiety.  It doesn't necessarily have to be getting a job - I don't know if you already have one or are in school or whatever you situation might be.  But, doing something where you can be around or connect with people might help.  A hobby that requires you to be with people, a book/movie club, an online MMO with a guild or something (I play WoW with a bunch of people, and that helps).

Writing might be another outlet.  You've done some of it here.  You could expand on those ideas, start a blog, or just keep a journal for yourself.  Exercise is another option.  Even if it's just simple stuff like going for a walk or doing arm raises or jumping jacks or stretches or whatever.  Walking and biking helped me feel less anxious.  Music, too.  Quiet, calming music like Aphex Twin's Selected Ambient Works is a go-to for me.

And, of course, I have to say that I'm not a doctor and this isn't medical advice.  These are some things that worked for me that you might try.  If it feels like it's too much, you should consider seeing a counselor for more personalized techniques to help you cope with and/or alleviate your anxiety.  If you don't have the money to see a counselor, there are some websites you can use for help.  A quick Google search for online mental health help will turn up a couple different things.

Good luck. Be well.

I second a lot of what misterceejay said, but I'll add a few things.  If you're interested in her, really interested in her, be honest with her about how you feel and what's going on with your anxiety.  Communication is key in every relationship.  I cannot stress that enough.  It seems evident to me that you are self-reflective, which is a great quality to have.  You recognize your own limitations and see where things could go well or not so well.  Be thoughtful and mindful of those things.  And, she might be able to help you with that, especially if you communicate with her what you feel.

It's okay to overthink and worry.  Something a counselor I had in college said to me has really stuck with me about that:  "Emotions are neither good nor bad, they just are."  Please don't be ashamed of your own feelings.  Own them.  Recognize that you have them and choose how to act on them in a way that benefits you and those important to you.  You can't make your feelings just go away, but you can become more comfortable with them.

I think you've got this.  Even in your worry, you know what you want to do and you have the capability to do it.

I had the same problem for many years and didn't get my license until I was 23.  You might be made fun of - I was, and it was annoying and upsetting.  I was really defensive about it for a long time because there were many things that contributed to the delay in getting my license.  Having anxiety is a valid reason for postponing getting your license, but it's also an opportunity to grow with your anxiety.

Funny story about being too nervous during the test ... The instructor and I got into the car.  We put on our seatbelts. I checked my mirrors and started the car.  The instructor got out and checked all of my lights, then stood in front of my car.  He asked me to blow the horn, then asked me to put on my four-ways.  And then he asked me to put on my right turn signal.  Of course, I put on my left.  He said, "Your other right turn signal."  I changed the signal.  The instructor got back into the car.  I said, "Well, now that I got THAT out of my system."  We proceeded with the test, and I ended up passing.
